rationale: This is an equal-weighted rank blend of two of the most heavily documented anomalies (Cooper-Gulen-Schill asset growth and Sloan/Richardson balance-sheet accruals) that are themselves strongly correlated and both largely spanned by the FF5 CMA factor, so it is a rediscovery/repackaging rather than a genuine interaction, and SUMRANK enforces additivity precisely where the hypothesis claims conditionality.

The composition idea (accounting growth per dollar of real investment) is reasonably fresh, but the construction is fragile — winsorizing the denominator at 1% still leaves near-zero and negative-accrual cases that make the ratio explode and flip sign non-monotonically, so cross-sectional ranks will be driven by low-capex firms rather than by growth composition; a bounded form (e.g., accruals minus capex, both scaled by assets, or a rank difference) would test the same economics far more cleanly.

The conditional design is internally consistent and is a legitimate sharpening test of whether the asset-growth effect concentrates in accrual-led expanders, but it creates a large mass point at exactly zero (all capex-dominated firms) that will dominate middle quantiles and make the long leg consist of accrual-dominated *shrinkers* rather than the "unpenalized" firms the hypothesis describes, and the use of oancf restricts coverage to post-1988.

Two defects: the growth rate of non-cash working capital is undefined/sign-flipping for the many firms with near-zero or negative working capital, and the positive expected sign requires the long leg to be high gross-PP&E-growth firms, which the well-established investment/CMA anomaly says underperform — so the stated sign fights the natural direction of the dominant leg.

The first leg is essentially the published inventory-growth anomaly (Thomas-Zhang, Belo-Lin), and the second leg is deliberately sign-flipped investment growth, so the composite goes long high-PP&E-growth firms in direct opposition to the documented investment effect — the two legs are likely to offset rather than reinforce, and the "capacity" conditioning would be better expressed as an interaction than as an additive rank sum.

Cumulating accruals over five years is close to a re-derivation of the net-operating-assets/balance-sheet-bloat anomaly (Hirshleifer et al.), and the negatively signed capex leg contradicts Fairfield-Whisenant-Yohn's finding that long-term operating-asset growth predicts returns with the same negative sign as accruals, so the differencing likely cancels signal instead of isolating composition.
